result.title: These are the 10 most gender equal countries in the world
result.description:
The first Global Gender Gap Report was published 20 years ago. After two decades of data on gender parity, it’s clear the world is travelling in the right direction.
  
Back in 2006, the average gender gap of the 97 economies that have featured in every report was 64% closed. Today it is 69% closed - a new high-water mark. 

For the third consecutive year, a higher number of economies have reported better results. The ranking tracks 14 indicators across health, education, economic participation and politics - and of those indicators, 10 have improved since last year.

The global gender gap in educational attainment is now 97% closed - and is on course to close fully in eight years’ time. 

How wide is the gender gap in your economy? Find out in the Global Gender Gap Report 2026: https://www.weforum.org/publications/global-gender-gap-report-2026

result.title: Has AI changed how you get your first job?
result.description:
Peter Brown, Global Workforce Leader at PwC, explains to the World Economic Forum’s Kateryna Gordiychuk how AI is changing the world of #work for entry-level job-seekers.

Entry-level jobs have traditionally helped young people build the #skills they need to progress. But according to PwC research, employers are now 7 times more likely to expect candidates to arrive with 'senior-level' skills.

Listen to the full conversation on our #MeetTheLeader podcast, exploring the report Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Entry-Level Work: https://open.spotify.com/episode/3QjJhkcHLrIlr3QcPpXqoT?si=9Nk9LnFVRXCS_2Bx7rg30Q&nd=1&dlsi=f77ef1ca63cb499e

result.title: The Race For Copper Supplies & The Company Tackling Fishing Net Waste | WEF | Stories of the Week
result.description:
00:12 - Meet the woman making safer batteries:
It was the forgotten idea of a Nobel-winning scientist. Now, Emilie Bodoin is turning it into reality. The Founder and CEO of Pure Lithium has revived the ‘lithium metal battery’ – an alternative to the lithium-ion batteries we know from electric vehicles, and a breakthrough that could make batteries lighter, safer and more efficient – all while reducing dependence on critical mineral supply chains.

04:08 - Why countries are scrambling for copper:
Why did Japan just lend $466 million to Chile’s state copper mining company? The answer lies in the energy transition. Whether it’s solar farms, data centres or electric vehicles, tomorrow’s infrastructure relies on critical minerals. And none is more crucial than copper, which is used almost anywhere electricity is generated, transmitted or used.

06:03 - Turning discarded nets into sportswear:
Fishing nets can take decades to break down - and when they’re lost at sea, they can entangle marine life and damage ocean habitats. Start-up Bureo collects discarded nets from around the world, then recycles them into nylon yarn for waterproof jackets, hats and sportswear.

result.title: 3 ways young people can prepare for work in a world of AI
result.description:
As AI’s capabilities expand, many entry-level #jobs are being impacted, leading to a wave of understandable concern about how young people will make their way in the world of #work.

Arun Sundararajan has some encouragement. As Professor of Entrepreneurship at NYU Stern School of Business, he advises students on how to stand out in a rapidly evolving labour market. From building human networks to becoming an AI ‘force multiplier’, here’s what he tells them.

Arun was speaking to the World Economic Forum's Robin Pomeroy and CGTN's Xin Guan for our Radio Davos video podcast. Watch the full episode: https://youtu.be/waYzMBSQuPo
